meta.title: Who really said "Every king springs from a race of slaves, and every slave has had kings among his ancestors"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Seneca really did write it — in Letter 44, where he credits Plato in the same breath. The famous English is Richard Gummere's 1917 Loeb translation.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Every king springs from a race of slaves, and every slave has had kings among his ancestors'?
meta.ogDescription: Yes, it's Seneca — Letter 44, §4 — and he opens it "Plato says". Plato's Theaetetus puts it far more loosely; the pithy English is Gummere's, 1917.

answer.label: Written by

answer.sourceLine: The sentence is genuinely Seneca’s, in his own Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium, Letter 44, §4 — and Seneca opens it with “Plato says”, crediting the thought to Plato as he writes it. The exact English now in circulation is Richard M. Gummere’s Loeb translation of 1917, confirmed on page 289 of the scanned volume ↗.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium, Letter 44 (“On Philosophy and Pedigrees”), §4
c. AD 62–65, in Latin, in Seneca’s last years
Richard M. Gummere, Loeb Classical Library, 1917 — vol. I, p. 289
Platon ait neminem regem non ex servis esse oriundum, neminem servum non ex regibus.

source.excerpt: We have all had the same number of forefathers; there is no man whose first beginning does not transcend memory. Plato says: “Every king springs from a race of slaves, and every slave has had kings among his ancestors.” The flight of time, with its vicissitudes, has jumbled all such things together, and Fortune has turned them upside down. Then who is well-born? He who is by nature well fitted for virtue.
trail: 4th century BC — Plato has Socrates observe that everyone’s ancestry contains “rich and poor, kings and slaves, barbarians and Greeks”, in Theaetetus 174e–175a ↗. The idea, not the epigram.
c. AD 62–65 — Seneca compresses it into one sentence in Letter 44 and attributes it to Plato: the Latin at §4 ↗.
1917 — Richard M. Gummere’s Loeb translation gives the sentence the English shape it now circulates in, on p. 289 of volume I ↗.
Today — it spreads under both names, often credited to Plato alone; Quote Investigator untangled the chain in 2020 ↗.
source.excerptNote: Gummere’s translation, Letter 44 §4–5. Note that Seneca puts the sentence in quotation marks and hands the credit to Plato before continuing in his own voice.

author.name: Seneca the Younger
author.kicker: The man who wrote it down
author.heading: Who was Seneca?
author.metaLine: c. 4 BC – AD 65 · Roman Stoic philosopher, statesman and dramatist
author.bio: Lucius Annaeus Seneca the Younger was a Stoic philosopher, statesman and tragedian of imperial Rome who served as tutor and then adviser to the emperor Nero — and was eventually ordered by him to die. After withdrawing from public life around AD 62 he wrote the Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium, 124 surviving letters of practical moral instruction composed in his last two or three years. Letter 44 is one of them: a short, bracing reply to a correspondent who felt held back by an unremarkable family name.

misattribution.heading: The fact-check
misattribution.intro: This one is genuine, but it travels under two different names and in wording that belongs to a third person. Three things are worth separating.

items.why: Quote sites routinely run the line as a Plato quote — Goodreads attributes it to Plato with no book named ↗ — because Seneca’s own sentence begins “Plato says”. But Plato never wrote this sentence. Gummere’s footnote sends the reader to Theaetetus 174e–175a ↗, where Socrates says only that everyone’s ancestors have included “rich and poor, kings and slaves, barbarians and Greeks.”

Quote Investigator concludes ↗ that the core idea was attributed to Socrates by Plato, and that Seneca “credited Plato with a restatement of this comment.” So the thought is Socratic; the epigram is Seneca’s compression of it.

Seneca’s Latin reads Platon ait neminem regem non ex servis esse oriundum, neminem servum non ex regibus — a chain of double negatives, closer to ‘no king is not descended from slaves, and no slave not from kings’. The balanced, quotable English is the translator’s work; the Latin is on the facing text at §4 ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Seneca did write it, in a letter he composed himself, and he credited the thought to Plato in the same sentence — which is why both names are attached to it. Quote Investigator’s trace ↗ runs Socrates → Plato’s Theaetetus → Seneca’s restatement, and the exact English words are Gummere’s 1917 rendering.

context.heading: Why Seneca wrote it
lead: Letter 44 answers a complaint. Seneca’s correspondent Lucilius has been running himself down — he is a Roman knight, not an aristocrat, and he feels that nature and fortune have short-changed him. Seneca’s reply is that philosophy, unlike Roman society, “never looks into pedigrees”: Socrates was no aristocrat, Cleanthes drew water for a living, and Plato was made noble by philosophy rather than found so.

The line about kings and slaves is the hinge of that argument. Push any family tree back far enough, Seneca says, and it dissolves into everybody else’s — so ancestry proves nothing, and the only useful question is who is “by nature well fitted for virtue.” It is an unusually egalitarian move from a man who was one of the richest in the empire.
detailsBody: Gummere prints the Latin with a note that the reading servum non is the emendation of the Danish scholar J. N. Madvig, while the manuscripts read non servum. The sense is unaffected; the sentence turns on a double negative in either form.

Gummere’s footnote to the sentence points the reader to Plato, Theaetetus 174e ↗. Read the two side by side and the difference is plain: Plato’s Socrates makes a diffuse point about the sheer number of everyone’s forebears; Seneca compresses it into an epigram.
context.pull: Philosophy did not find Plato already a nobleman; it made him one.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator concludes the core idea was attributed to Socrates by Plato, that Seneca credited Plato with a restatement giving the exact wording 'Every king springs from a race of slaves, and every slave has had kings among his ancestors', and that Helen Keller later echoed it.

Wikisource's Gummere translation of Seneca's Letter 44 contains 'Plato says: Every king springs from a race of slaves, and every slave has had kings among his ancestors', followed by 'The flight of time, with its vicissitudes, has jumbled all such things together, and Fortune has turned them upside down.'

The full scanned text of the Loeb edition contains, at Epistle XLIV, the English 'Plato says: "Every king springs from a race of slaves, and every slave has had kings among his ancestors."' on p. 289, the facing Latin 'Platon ait neminem regem non ex servis esse oriundum, neminem servum non ex regibus' on p. 288, the apparatus note 'servum non Madvig; non servum MSS.', the footnote 'Plato, Theaetetus, p. 174 e.', the letter title 'XLIV. ON PHILOSOPHY AND PEDIGREES', and the sentence 'Philosophy did not find Plato already a nobleman; it made him one.'

The Internet Archive record identifies this volume as 'Ad Lucilium epistulae morales. With an English translation by Richard M. Gummere', Seneca (ca. 4 B.C.–65 A.D), volume 1, publisher London: Heinemann, publication date 1917.

Perseus's text of Plato's Theaetetus 175a, in Harold N. Fowler's translation (Plato in Twelve Volumes, Vol. 12, Harvard University Press, 1921), contains the phrase 'among whom have been in any instance rich and poor, kings and slaves, barbarians and Greeks.'
The Latin text of Seneca's Letter 44 is numbered in sections, and the sentence 'Platon ait neminem regem non ex servis esse oriundum...' falls in section [4].
Goodreads runs this quote attributed to Plato, with no book named on the page.

The Perseus Catalog record for the English Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium gives translator Richard M. Gummere, publisher Harvard University Press and Heinemann, series Loeb Classical Library, volume I (Books I–LXV), date of publication 1917.

Wikipedia states the Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium comprise 124 extant letters written in the last two or three years of Seneca's life, after his retirement from public office around spring AD 62.
